71.quote_or_event: “I cannot survive without seeing my Beloved. My eyes are welling up with tears.”
71.explanation: In a Maajh hymn of longing, Guru Ram Das describes love for the Beloved Lord that cannot be held in silence: separation shows itself at once in tears.
71.tie_back: Like Valluvar's single tear, the welling eyes are the outward proof that betrays a love the heart could not lock inside.
71.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 94, Raag Maajh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
71._accuracy_note: Strong match on tears as the visible sign of love, but the Gurbani love is devotional longing for God, while the Kural speaks of tears shed for a suffering loved one.

72.quote_or_event: “Why do you say, "Mine, mine"? Look to God, who has given it to you.”
72.explanation: Guru Arjan diagnoses the possessive cry of mine, mine as a symptom of moh (attachment), one of the five thieves, and reminds the listener that everything held was given and is not truly owned.
72.tie_back: It answers the first half of the Kural exactly: the loveless claim everything as their own, and Gurbani names that claim as the false root to be uprooted.
72.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 50, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
72._accuracy_note: Good parallel for the possessive half of the couplet; the verse does not itself picture the loving person giving even their bones to others, which is the Kural's second and more striking claim.

73.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe.”
73.explanation: In a hymn recited daily in the Sikh evening prayer, Guru Arjan teaches that human birth is a rare gift whose whole purpose is loving union with God.
73.tie_back: Both texts give embodiment a reason: the precious life takes a body in order to live out love.
73.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (So Purakh section of Rehras), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
73._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel on the purpose of embodiment; in Gurbani that purpose is union with God through the Name, whereas the Kural speaks of love (anbu) more broadly, including love between people.

74.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
74.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the change that comes from the company of the holy (sadh sangat): once love has replaced jealousy, everyone becomes a friend and no one remains an outsider.
74.tie_back: As in the Kural's chain from love to warm eagerness to friendship, friendship here is not pursued but arrives as the by-product of a heart already changed by love.
74.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
74._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on universal friendship flowing from inner transformation, but the hymn credits the holy congregation, not a stated chain from love through eagerness to friendship.

75.quote_or_event: “Sing, and listen, and let your mind be filled with love. Your pain shall be sent far away, and peace shall come to your home.”
75.explanation: In the Japji, the opening hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak promises that a mind settled in love brings peace into the home here and now.
75.tie_back: It mirrors Valluvar's claim that the happiness of those who live well in this world is simply the fruit of a life settled in love.
75.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, Pauri 5, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
75._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit with this-worldly peace as love's fruit; the love in the Japji is directed to God through praise, while the Kural's love is a general disposition toward others.

76.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. … give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
76.explanation: Guru Nanak makes love of God a path that demands total self-offering; Sikh tradition sees this ideal enacted when Guru Gobind Singh, founding the Khalsa in 1699, asked for volunteers ready to give their heads, joining devotion to the courage to defend others.
76.tie_back: It supports Valluvar's counter-intuitive point that love is the companion not only of virtue but of fearless, even martial, valour.
76.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek (salok 20), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
76._accuracy_note: The Sikh fusion of love and courage (saint-soldier) is a genuine parallel, but the verse itself speaks of spiritual self-surrender; the martial link comes from the later Khalsa tradition, not the verse's own words.

77.quote_or_event: “Without love, there is no devotional worship. Without the Shabad, no one finds acceptance.”
77.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that religious practice emptied of love has no standing before God; the loveless soul is simply not accepted in the divine order.
77.tie_back: It shares the Kural's verdict that, without love, a life cannot stand up to the moral order meant to sustain it.
77.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 67, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
77._accuracy_note: Next-best match only: the verse shares the idea that love is indispensable, but lacks the Kural's vivid image of righteousness scorching the loveless like the sun scorching a boneless worm.

78.quote_or_event: “My body is like the simmal tree; seeing me, other people are fooled.”
78.explanation: Guru Nanak compares a life lacking true virtue to the tall, imposing simmal (silk-cotton) tree, whose appearance promises fruit that never satisfies.
78.tie_back: Like Valluvar's dead tree putting out shoots in the desert, it pictures a life with the look of flourishing but nothing real inside.
78.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
78._accuracy_note: Strong match on the tree image of hollow outward flourishing; the hymn's lack is of virtue and the Name in general rather than of love specifically.

79.quote_or_event: “Without her Husband, the soul-bride's youth and ornaments are useless and wretched.”
79.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the bride-soul image: without the inner bond of love with the Husband Lord, all outward beauty and adornment serve no purpose.
79.tie_back: As the Kural asks what good the outer limbs are without love as the inner organ, Gurbani declares outer endowments useless without the inner relationship.
79.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 58, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
79._accuracy_note: Good fit on outer versus inner, but the love meant is spiritual love for God expressed through the bride image, not the Kural's general love, and ornaments are not bodily organs.

80.quote_or_event: “Fareed, that body, within which love of the Lord does not well up - look upon that body as a cremation ground.”
80.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sufi saint Sheikh Farid declares that a body in which love does not arise is not truly alive but a place of the dead.
80.tie_back: It is almost exactly the Kural's verdict: without love, the body is mere bone wrapped in skin, a corpse rather than the seat of life.
80.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
80._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: a loveless body counted as dead; the only difference is that Farid's love (birha) is love and longing for God rather than love for people.
